stem:
Ascent, Assent, Accent
1. The Sherpas guided the team during their treacherous ascent of Mt. Everest.
2. The President has given his assent to the new education bill.
3. His British accent made it difficult for the local villagers to understand him.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Ascent is a climb upward, assent is agreement or official approval, and accent is a manner of pronunciation. The Everest climb, the President approving a bill and the British pronunciation each use the right word, so all three sentences are correct. Matches option D.

stem:
Altar, Alter
1. The priest placed the sacred offerings on the alter.
2. We had to altar our travel plans due to the sudden heavy snowfall.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Altar is the noun for a raised table used in worship, while alter is the verb meaning to change. Sentence 1 needs altar but prints alter, and sentence 2 needs alter but prints altar, so both are wrong. Matches option D.

stem:
Ingenious, Ingenuous, Disingenuous
1. The military engineer devised an ingenious bridge-building technique under fire.
2. The ingenuous recruit believed everything the seniors told him as a prank.
3. It would be disingenuous of the politician to claim he knew nothing about the scandal.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Ingenious means cleverly inventive, ingenuous means innocently trusting, and disingenuous means insincere or pretending ignorance. The inventive engineer, the gullible recruit and the politician feigning ignorance each fit, so all three are correct. Matches option D.

stem:
Perspective, Prospective, Retrospective
1. Traveling provides a broader perspective on global cultures.
2. The firm is currently interviewing prospective candidates for the manager's post.
3. The board conducted a retrospective study of the project's failures.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Perspective is a point of view, prospective means likely or expected in the future, and retrospective means looking back at past events. A broader view of cultures, candidates yet to be hired and a study of past failures all match their words. Matches option D.

stem:
Accede, Exceed
1. The authorities refused to accede to the demands of the protestors.
2. Drivers are warned not to exceed the speed limit on the expressway.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Accede means to agree to a demand or request, while exceed means to go beyond a limit. Refusing to agree to the protestors and going over the speed limit both use the correct word. Matches option C.

stem:
Loath (Adjective), Loathe (Verb)
1. He was loathe to admit that he had made a significant error in the calculations.
2. Many people loathe the idea of working on weekends.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Loath is the adjective meaning reluctant, and it follows the verb was; loathe is the verb meaning to hate. Sentence 1 needs the adjective loath but prints the verb form loathe, while sentence 2 correctly uses loathe as a verb. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Arguable: some dictionaries list loathe as a variant spelling of the adjective loath, which would make sentence 1 defensible and the answer C. Rejected because the item itself labels the set Loath (Adjective), Loathe (Verb), so the printed spelling in sentence 1 violates the distinction the question is testing.

stem:
Judicial, Judicious, Judiciary
1. The case will undergo a judicial review to ensure all protocols were followed.
2. A judicious manager knows when to delegate tasks and when to intervene.
3. The judiciary is one of the three main pillars of a democratic government.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Judicial relates to courts and legal judgement, judicious means showing good sense, and the judiciary is the body of judges as an institution. A court review, a sensible manager and the third pillar of government each take the right word. Matches option D.

stem:
Amiable, Amicable
1. The new neighbor is very amiable and always greets us with a smile.
2. After months of tension, the two nations finally reached an amicable settlement.
3. The principal is known for his amicable personality, making students feel at ease.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Amiable describes a person with a friendly disposition, while amicable describes a relationship, agreement or settlement reached without hostility. Sentences 1 and 2 are correct, but sentence 3 applies amicable to a personality where amiable is required. Matches option A.

stem:
Defuse, Diffuse
1. The bomb disposal squad worked quickly to defuse the explosive.
2. The fragrance of the lilies began to defuse throughout the garden.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Defuse means to remove the fuse from a bomb or to reduce tension, while diffuse means to spread out over an area. Sentence 1 is correct, but a fragrance spreading through a garden needs diffuse, not defuse. Matches option A.

stem:
Affect (Verb), Effect (Noun)
1. The pollution in the city will seriously affect the health of the residents.
2. The new government policy had an immediate effect on the stock market.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Affect is the verb meaning to influence, and effect is the noun meaning a result. Pollution influencing health takes the verb, and an immediate result on the market takes the noun, so both are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Historic, Historical
1. The moon landing was a historic event for all of mankind.
2. The museum is filled with historical artifacts from the Roman Empire.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Historic means famous or important in history, while historical simply means belonging to or concerning the past. The moon landing was momentous and the Roman artifacts are objects from the past, so both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Economic, Economical
1. The country is currently facing a severe economic crisis.
2. This new electric car is very economical to maintain.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Economic relates to the economy or to finance in general, while economical means thrifty or inexpensive to run. A national crisis of the economy and a car that is cheap to maintain each use the right word. Matches option C.

stem:
Allusion, Illusion
1. The novel is full of allusions to Greek mythology.
2. The magician created the illusion that the lady was floating in the air.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: An allusion is an indirect reference to something, while an illusion is a false or deceptive appearance. References to Greek mythology and a magician's deceptive floating trick both fit their words. Matches option C.

stem:
Censure, Sensor, Censor
1. The opposition moved a motion to censure the government for the price hike.
2. The movie was sent to the board to censure the violent scenes.
3. The automatic door operates using a motion sensor.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Censure means to criticise formally, censor means to remove objectionable material, and a sensor is a device that detects. Sentences 1 and 3 are correct, but cutting violent scenes requires censor, not censure. Matches option B.

stem:
Hoard, Horde
1. During the war, some people began to hoard essential supplies.
2. A horde of tourists descended on the small village during the summer.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Hoard is to store up a hidden supply, while a horde is a large crowd. Stockpiling supplies in wartime and a crowd of tourists each take the correct word. Matches option C.

stem:
Tortuous, Torturous
1. The mountain path was tortuous, with many sharp bends and narrow passes.
2. The long wait for the exam results was a tortuous experience for the students.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Tortuous means full of twists and bends, while torturous means causing pain or suffering. Sentence 1 correctly describes a winding path, but the agonising wait for results needs torturous, not tortuous. Matches option A.

stem:
Emigrate, Immigrate
1. Due to the civil war, many families decided to emigrate from their home country.
2. My uncle plans to immigrate to Canada in search of better job opportunities.
3. The government has introduced strict laws for those who wish to emigrate into the country.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Emigrate is to leave one country, and immigrate is to come into another. Sentences 1 and 2 are correct, but sentence 3 pairs emigrate with into the country, where immigrate is required. Matches option A.

stem:
Envelop (Verb), Envelope (Noun)
1. The thick morning mist seemed to envelop the entire valley.
2. Please place the formal invitation inside the silk envelope.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Envelop is the verb meaning to wrap or surround completely, while an envelope is the paper cover for a letter. Mist surrounding the valley takes the verb and the invitation goes inside the noun, so both are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Foreword, Forward
1. The famous historian wrote a brilliant forword for the new book.
2. The troops were ordered to move foreward despite the heavy rain.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: A foreword is the introductory note at the front of a book, while forward means onward or ahead. As printed both sentences misspell their words, giving forword in sentence 1 and foreward in sentence 2, so neither is correct. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Arguable: if the misspellings are read charitably as the intended words, both sentences use the right word for the sense and the answer would be C. Rejected because the printed forms forword and foreward are not English words at all, and the rule is to answer as printed.

stem:
Flout, Flaunt
1. Many motorists continue to flout traffic rules despite the heavy fines.
2. He loves to flaunt his expensive watches at every social gathering.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Flout means to openly disobey a rule, while flaunt means to display something showily. Motorists disobeying traffic rules and a man showing off his watches both use the correct word. Matches option C.

stem:
Hail, Hale
1. The heavy hail storm damaged the crops in the northern plains.
2. My grandfather is eighty years old but still hale and hearty.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Hail is frozen rain falling in pellets, so a hail storm damaging crops is right. Hale is an adjective meaning strong and healthy, especially in old age, which fits the idiom hale and hearty. Both sentences use their word correctly. Matches option C.

stem:
Lightning, Lightening
1. The dark clouds were followed by a sudden flash of lightning.
2. They are lightening the cargo of the ship to help it float better.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Lightning is the electrical flash in a storm and takes no letter e in the middle. Lightening is the participle of lighten, meaning to make less heavy, which is exactly what reducing a ship's load does. Both are used correctly. Matches option C.

stem:
Ascetic, Aesthetic
1. The monk led an ascetic life, renouncing all worldly pleasures.
2. The interior designer was praised for the aesthetic appeal of the office.
3. His ascetic appreciation for art made him a great critic.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Ascetic means severely self denying, so the monk renouncing worldly pleasures is correct, and aesthetic means concerned with beauty, which fits the designer's work. Sentence 3 needs aesthetic, since appreciation of art is a sense of beauty and not a life of self denial. Only 1 and 2 are correct. Matches option A.

stem:
Precede, Proceed
1. A brief moment of silence will precede the national anthem.
2. After the briefing, the commandos were told to proceed with the mission.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Precede means to come before something in time or order, so silence preceding the anthem is right. Proceed means to go forward or begin, which fits the commandos starting their mission. Both are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Credible, Credulous
1. The evidence presented in court was not considered credible by the judge.
2. He is so credulous that he believes every conspiracy theory he reads online.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Credible describes the thing believed and means worthy of belief, so evidence the judge doubted is not credible. Credulous describes the person believing and means too willing to believe, which fits someone who accepts every conspiracy theory. Both are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Persecute, Prosecute
1. Throughout history, many groups have been persecuted for their religious beliefs.
2. The crown attorney decided to prosecute the suspect for grand larceny.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Persecute means to oppress or ill treat someone, typically for their beliefs or identity. Prosecute means to bring legal proceedings against someone in court, which is what a crown attorney does. Both sentences use the right word. Matches option C.

stem:
Cereal, Serial
1. Corn and wheat are common types of serial crops.
2. The detective realized they were dealing with a cereal offender.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: The two words have been swapped. Cereal means an edible grain such as corn or wheat, so sentence 1 should read cereal crops, while serial means occurring in a repeated series, so sentence 2 should read serial offender. Neither sentence is correct. Matches option D.

stem:
Waver, Waiver
1. His commitment to the cause did not waver despite the threats.
2. You must sign a waiver before participating in the bungee jump.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Waver is a verb meaning to falter or become unsteady, which fits a commitment that held firm under threat. Waiver is a noun meaning a document giving up a right or claim, which is what a bungee operator asks you to sign. Both are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Luxuriant, Luxurious, Luxuriate
1. The tropical rainforest is known for its luxuriant vegetation and diverse wildlife.
2. The delegation stayed in a luxurious hotel during the international summit.
3. After a week of hard training, the soldiers were allowed to luxuriate in a hot bath.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Luxuriant means growing thickly and abundantly, which is why it suits rainforest vegetation rather than expense. Luxurious means costly and comfortable, fitting the hotel, and luxuriate is the verb meaning to take great pleasure in something, fitting the soldiers in a hot bath. All three are correct. Matches option D.

stem:
Element, Elemental, Elementary
1. Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe.
2. The survivors had to brave the elemental fury of the mountain storm.
3. Solving this equation requires only elementary knowledge of algebra.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: An element is a basic substance such as hydrogen, elemental describes the raw primal forces of nature such as a storm, and elementary means basic or introductory, fitting simple algebra. Each sentence uses the right member of the set. Matches option D.

stem:
Official, Officious, Officiate
1. The department received an official letter from the Ministry of Defence.
2. The shopkeeper was rather officious, constantly telling customers what they should buy.
3. A senior referee was called in to officiate the final football match.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Official means authorised or formal, fitting a Ministry letter, while officious means annoyingly eager to give unwanted orders or advice, fitting the interfering shopkeeper. Officiate is the verb meaning to act as an official or referee at an event. All three are correct. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Arguable only on sentence 3. The traditional construction is officiate AT a match, and a strict prescriptivist would call the transitive officiate the match loose, which would give option A. Rejected because major dictionaries now record officiate as transitive in sporting use (to officiate a game), and the word is in any case not confused with official or officious, which is the distinction being tested.

stem:
Flagrant, Fragrant, Vagrant
1. The player was sent off for a flagrant violation of the safety rules.
2. The garden was filled with the fragrant scent of blooming jasmine.
3. The police questioned the vagrant found sleeping under the bridge.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Flagrant means blatant and openly shocking, fitting a rule violation, fragrant means sweet smelling, fitting jasmine, and a vagrant is a person with no settled home. The three near identical spellings carry completely unrelated meanings, and each is placed correctly here. Matches option D.

stem:
Ethereal, Ephemeral, Euphemism
1. The bride looked almost ethereal in the soft morning light.
2. Fame in the world of social media is often ephemeral, lasting only a few days.
3. "Passed away" is a common euphemism for the word "died."
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Ethereal means delicate and unearthly, fitting the bride in soft light, while ephemeral means short lived, fitting fleeting social media fame. A euphemism is a mild expression substituted for a blunt one, and passed away for died is the standard example. All three are correct. Matches option D.

stem:
Abate, Abet, Abjure
1. The floodwaters began to abate after the rain stopped.
2. He was found guilty of aiding and abetting the crime.
3. The witness was asked to abjure his previous false testimony in court.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Abate means to lessen in intensity, fitting receding floodwaters, and abet means to help someone commit a crime, fitting the legal phrase aiding and abetting. Abjure means to renounce something solemnly or on oath, which is what a witness does when formally disowning earlier false testimony. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Arguable only on sentence 3. Recant is the precise term for withdrawing testimony, and abjure most often takes a belief, claim or allegiance as its object, so a strict reader could call sentence 3 loose and choose option A. Rejected because abjure is defined as to renounce upon oath or repudiate solemnly, which covers a sworn disavowal made in court.

stem:
Obviate, Obliterate, Obfuscate
1. Thorough preparation can obviate the need for last-minute revisions.
2. The heavy artillery fire managed to obliterate the enemy bunkers.
3. The politician tried to obfuscate the truth by using technical jargon.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Obviate means to make something unnecessary, so preparation obviating last minute revision is right. Obliterate means to destroy utterly, fitting artillery on bunkers, and obfuscate means to make deliberately unclear, fitting a politician hiding behind jargon. All three are correct. Matches option D.

stem:
Allay, Alley, Ally
1. The Prime Minister's speech helped to allay the fears of the public regarding the economy.
2. The suspect escaped by running down a narrow, dark alley behind the market.
3. France was a key ally during the historic military campaign.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Allay is a verb meaning to calm or reduce fear, alley is a noun meaning a narrow passage between buildings, and ally is a noun meaning a partner or supporting nation. Each of the three sentences uses the correct part of speech and meaning. Matches option D.

stem:
Inveterate, Invertebrate
1. He is an inveterate gambler who simply cannot stay away from the casino.
2. An invertebrate is an animal, such as an insect or mollusk, that lacks a backbone.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Inveterate means long established in a habit and unlikely to change, which fits a compulsive gambler. Invertebrate is a noun for an animal without a backbone, such as an insect or mollusc. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Callous, Callow
1. The dictator showed a callous disregard for the suffering of his people.
2. The callow youth had much to learn about the complexities of international politics.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Callous means hardened and unfeeling towards the suffering of others, fitting the dictator. Callow means immature and inexperienced, fitting a young person with much to learn. Both are used correctly. Matches option C.

stem:
Forbear (Verb), Forebear (Noun)
1. He decided to forbear from making any further comments until the facts were clear.
2. My forebears originally came from a small village in the mountains of Scotland.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Forbear is the verb meaning to hold back or refrain from doing something, which fits declining to comment further. Forebear is the noun meaning an ancestor, which fits family who came from a Scottish village. The extra letter e marks the noun, and both sentences follow that split. Matches option C.

stem:
Mendacious, Meretricious
1. The witness was cross-examined for providing mendacious statements to the police.
2. The room was decorated in a meretricious style that looked expensive but was actually quite cheap.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Mendacious means lying or untruthful, fitting a witness giving false statements to the police. Meretricious means showily attractive but cheap and insincere, fitting decor that only looks expensive. Both are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Obsequious, Obsequies
1. The manager was surrounded by obsequious assistants who agreed with everything he said.
2. The royal family gathered to perform the final obsequies for the late King.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Obsequious means excessively fawning or servile, which fits assistants who agree with everything the manager says; obsequies are funeral rites, which fits a ceremony for a dead king. Both sentences place their word correctly. Matches option C.

stem:
Profligate, Prolific
1. The government was criticized for its profligate spending on unnecessary projects.
2. The prolific author managed to publish three novels in a single year.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Profligate means recklessly wasteful, so it fits spending criticised as unnecessary; prolific means producing a great deal, so it fits an author with three novels in one year. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Temerity, Timidity
1. He had the temerity to challenge the commander's decision in front of the entire unit.
2. The recruit's timidity prevented him from speaking up during the tactical briefing.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Temerity is reckless boldness or nerve, which fits challenging a commander in front of the unit; timidity is a lack of confidence, which fits a recruit who will not speak up. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Turbid, Turgid
1. The river became turbid after the heavy silt was stirred up by the storm.
2. The scholar's writing style was criticized for being overly turgid and difficult to follow.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Turbid describes a liquid made cloudy by stirred-up sediment, which fits a silt-laden river; turgid describes prose that is swollen and pompous, which fits a style that is hard to follow. The two words differ by one letter but never overlap in sense, and each is used correctly here. Matches option C.

stem:
Perspicuous, Perspicacious
1. The manual provided a perspicuous explanation of the complex machinery.
2. The perspicacious detective immediately noticed the inconsistency in the alibi.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Perspicuous means clearly expressed and easy to follow, which describes the manual; perspicacious means mentally sharp and quick to notice, which describes the detective. One word praises the expression, the other the mind, and each is correctly placed. Matches option C.

stem:
Contiguous, Contingent
1. The United States consists of 48 contiguous states located on the North American continent.
2. The success of the mission is contingent upon the timely arrival of reinforcements.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Contiguous means sharing a border or touching, which is why the 48 mainland states are described that way; contingent means dependent on a condition, which fits a mission that depends on reinforcements arriving. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Iniquity, Inequity
1. The prophet spoke out against the iniquity and corruption of the royal court.
2. The strike was a protest against the gross inequity in the company's pay structure.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Iniquity means wickedness or gross immorality, which fits a corrupt court denounced by a prophet; inequity means unfairness or unequal treatment, which fits an unjust pay structure. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Reify, Rectify
1. It is a mistake to reify abstract concepts like "the economy" as if they were physical objects.
2. The technician was sent to rectify the error in the satellite's transmission code.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: To reify is to treat an abstraction as though it were a concrete thing, which is exactly the mistake the first sentence warns against; to rectify is to put right or correct, which fits repairing a faulty transmission code. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Abnegation, Negation
1. The monk's life was defined by the abnegation of all material desires and personal comforts.
2. The scientific discovery was a direct negation of the long-held theory about planetary orbits.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Abnegation is the renunciation or self-denial of something one could have, which fits a monk giving up material comforts; negation is the contradiction or nullifying of something, which fits a discovery that overturns an established theory. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Liminal, Subliminal
1. The hallway felt like a liminal space, existing somewhere between the entrance and the destination.
2. The advertisement used subliminal messages that were too fast for the conscious mind to perceive.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Liminal means occupying a threshold or in-between position, which fits a hallway lying between entrance and destination; subliminal means below the threshold of conscious awareness, which fits messages too fast to be consciously perceived. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Rack, Wrack
1. The prisoner was put on the rack to extract a confession.
2. The coastline was wracked by the most violent storm of the century.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: The rack was an instrument of torture that stretched the body, so the first sentence uses the literal noun correctly; to wrack is to wreck or devastate, which fits a coastline battered by a violent storm. Both sentences are correct. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Arguable. Some usage guides restrict wrack and would write racked by a storm, treating rack as the only verb. Wrack in the sense of wreck or lay waste is well established for physical destruction by weather (storm-wracked), so sentence 2 is accepted here.

stem:
Stanch (Verb), Staunch (Adjective)
1. The medic used a tourniquet to stanch the flow of blood from the soldier's leg.
2. He has been a staunch supporter of the environmental movement for over thirty years.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: To stanch is a verb meaning to stop a flow, especially of blood, which fits the tourniquet; staunch is an adjective meaning firm and loyal, which fits a supporter of thirty years. Each word appears in the part of speech the question specifies. Matches option C.

stem:
Strait, Straight
1. The children walked in a straight line.
2. He kept a strait face while hiding the joke.
3. Ships passed through the narrow strait between the islands.
Select the correct usage:
solution: Straight means without a bend or deviation, so the line in sentence 1 is right, and the idiom in sentence 2 should also be a straight face, not a strait one. A strait is a narrow channel of water between land masses, which sentence 3 uses correctly. Only sentences 1 and 3 are right. Matches option C.

stem:
Taut, Taught, Taunt
1. The rope must be pulled taught before climbing.
2. He taut physics for nearly ten years.
3. Rivals began to taunt him during the match.
Correct usage:
solution: Taut means pulled tight, so sentence 1 should read taut rather than taught; taught is the past tense of teach, so sentence 2 should read taught rather than taut. Taunt means to jeer at or provoke someone, which sentence 3 uses correctly. Only sentence 3 is right. Matches option C.

stem:
Vain, Vein, Vane
1. The nurse located a suitable vein for the injection.
2. The weather vain on the rooftop rotated wildly.
3. He made a vane attempt to lift the log by himself.
4. This might sound vain, but I know I'm better than she is.
Correct combination:
solution: A vein is a blood vessel, so sentence 1 is right, and vain meaning conceited fits sentence 4. Sentence 2 needs vane, the rotating pointer on a rooftop, and sentence 3 needs vain in its other sense of futile or useless. Only sentences 1 and 4 are correct. Matches option B.

stem:
Gambit, Gamut
1. His opening gambit immediately put the opponent on the defensive.
2. The festival showcased the entire gamut of local art.
Choose:
solution: A gambit is an opening move designed to gain an advantage, which fits putting an opponent on the defensive; a gamut is the complete range of something, which fits a festival covering all local art. Both sentences are correct. Matches option B.

stem: Reign, Rein
optA: Reign means control by pulling; Rein means royal authority.
optB: Reign means rule; Rein means to restrain or guide.
optC: Reign means punish; Rein means encourage.
solution: Reign is royal rule or the period of a monarch's authority, while a rein is the strap used to control a horse, giving the verb sense of restraining or guiding as in rein in. Option B states each meaning correctly, whereas the others swap or merge them. Matches option B.

stem:
Root, Rout, Route, Rut
1. The army suffered a humiliating rut.
2. They charted a direct route to the summit.
3. He attempted to root out corruption.
4. The film industry seemed to be stuck in a rout.
Correct usage:
solution: A rout is a crushing defeat and a rut is a dull fixed routine, so the first sentence needs rout and the fourth needs rut, and each has taken the other's word. A route is a planned way to a destination and to root out is to remove something at its source, so the second and third sentences are correct. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Source defect. The paper prints these four sentences without numbers while its options refer to 2 and 3 only, so the sentences are numbered 1 to 4 in printed order, which is the only available reading.

stem: Expatiate, Expiate
optA: Expatiate means to elaborate; Expiate means to atone.
optB: Expatiate means to atone; Expiate means to elaborate.
solution: To expatiate is to speak or write at length on a subject, while to expiate is to make amends or atone for a wrong. The correct option pairs each word with its own meaning; the closest distractor simply reverses them. Matches option A.

stem:
Tort, Torte, Tart
1. The bakery's famous chocolate torte sold out quickly.
2. The plaintiff filed a tart for damages.
3. Her mother's apple tort was loved by all.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used correctly?
solution: A torte is a rich layered cake, so sentence 1 is right; a tort is a civil wrong that gives rise to a legal claim, so sentence 2 should read tort rather than tart; a tart is an open pastry, so sentence 3 should read tart rather than tort. Only sentence 1 is correct. Matches option A.

stem:
Depredate, Depreciate, Decrepitate
1. The value of fixed assets depreciates over time.
2. Raiders would often depredate villages along the coast.
3. The logs began to decrepitate in the bonfire.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used correctly?
solution: Depreciate means to fall in value, depredate means to plunder or lay waste, and decrepitate means to crackle when strongly heated. Each sentence applies its word in exactly that sense, so all three are used correctly. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Decrepitate is most strictly used of salts and minerals crackling under heat, so applying it to logs stretches its technical range; it still matches the core sense of crackling on being heated, and the rival reading would give 1 and 2 only, option A. Accepted as correct because the sentence uses the word's real definition rather than confusing it with decrepit.

stem:
Gratuitous, Gratuity
1. The violence in the film was gratuitous.
2. He received a gratuity upon retirement.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used correctly?
solution: Gratuitous is an adjective meaning uncalled for or unwarranted, while gratuity is a noun meaning a tip or a sum paid on retirement. Both sentences use their word in the right sense and the right part of speech. Matches option C.

stem:
Inure, Ensure, Insure
1. Rigorous training will inure soldiers to hardships.
2. The manager sought to insure transparency.
3. They decided to ensure the building.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used correctly?
solution: Inure means to harden or accustom someone to something unpleasant, ensure means to make certain, and insure means to arrange financial cover. Only sentence 1 is right: sentence 2 needs ensure for making transparency certain, and sentence 3 needs insure for taking out a policy on a building. Matches option A.
reviewNote: American usage sometimes tolerates insure for ensure, which would make sentence 2 defensible; but no option offers 1 and 2 only, and sentence 3 is wrong on any reading, so A stands as the only consistent key.

stem:
Opposite, Apposite
1. His house was opposite a park.
2. His remark was perfectly apposite to the discussion.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used correctly?
solution: Opposite means facing or across from, while apposite means apt and strikingly appropriate to the matter in hand. Both sentences use their word correctly. Matches option C.

stem:
Weft, Wet, Whet
1. The smith used water to weft the blade.
2. Rain made the barn roof wet.
3. The weaver whet threads cross the warp on the loom.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used incorrectly?
solution: Whet means to sharpen, wet means soaked with liquid, and weft is the crosswise thread woven across the warp. The question asks for incorrect uses: sentences 1 and 3 have swapped whet and weft, while sentence 2 is correct. Matches option C.

stem:
Blight, Blithe
1. The crop blight ruined the harvest.
2. She remained blight despite the warnings.
3. His blithe manner calmed the crowd.
In which of the sentences has/have the words been used correctly?
solution: Blight is a plant disease or anything that spoils, while blithe means carefree and cheerful. Sentences 1 and 3 are right; sentence 2 needs blithe, since a person unbothered by warnings is carefree, not a disease. Matches option A.

stem: Conscience and Conscious
optA: Conscience means awareness and Conscious means moral sense
optB: Conscience means guilt and Conscious means shame
optC: Conscience means moral sense and Conscious means aware
optD: Conscience means deliberate and Conscious means ethical
solution: Conscience is the noun for a person's inner sense of right and wrong, while conscious is the adjective meaning awake or aware. Only one option pairs each word with its own meaning instead of reversing them. Matches option C.

stem: Beside and Besides
optA: Beside means in addition to, Besides means next to
optB: Beside means apart from, Besides means under
optC: Beside means except for, Besides means against
optD: Beside means next to, Besides means in addition to
solution: Beside is a preposition meaning next to or at the side of, while besides means in addition to or apart from. The first option states the pair the wrong way round. Matches option D.

stem: Esoteric and Exoteric
optA: Esoteric means abstruse and complicated, Exoteric means secret
optB: Esoteric means meant for select few, Exoteric means for general public
optC: Esoteric means ancient, Exoteric means modern
optD: Esoteric means scientific, Exoteric means spiritual
solution: Esoteric describes knowledge meant for and understood by a small initiated group, while exoteric describes what is suitable for the general public. Exoteric is not a synonym for secret, which rules out the first option. Matches option B.

stem: Elicit and Illicit
optA: Elicit means unlawful, and Illicit means to draw out.
optB: Elicit means to draw out, and Illicit means unlawful.
optC: Elicit means to hide, and Illicit means legal.
optD: Elicit means to approve, and Illicit means forbidden
solution: Elicit is a verb meaning to draw out a response or information, while illicit is an adjective meaning unlawful or forbidden. Matches option B.

stem:
Till vs Until
S1: We'll continue to work on this issue till we achieve a satisfactory resolution.
S2: He stayed awake all night, until he completed the final draft of his novel.
optA: S1 is right and S2 is wrong
optB: S1 is wrong and S2 is right
optC: Both S1 and S2 are wrong
optD: Both S1 and S2 are right
solution: Till and until are interchangeable in standard English, both meaning up to the time that; till is a word in its own right, not a clipped form of until, and is only a shade less formal. Each sentence uses its word correctly, so both are right. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Arguable item. Two rival readings were considered and rejected. First, that till is too informal for the register of S1: that is a stylistic preference, not an error, and usage guides do not call it wrong. Second, that S2 is faulty because staying awake all night sits oddly with an until clause implying he stopped once he finished: that is a semantic quibble about all night, not a till-versus-until distinction, and the word set names the pair under test. Since neither word could be swapped for the other to produce an error, both sentences stand and D is the key.

stem:
Curb vs Kerb
Statement 1: Curb means something that checks or restraints.
Statement 2: Kerb means raised edge between the pavement and the roadway.
solution: Curb is something that checks or restrains, and also the verb for doing so; kerb is the British spelling for the raised stone edge separating footpath from roadway. Both statements gloss their word correctly. Matches option A.

stem:
Beatific vs Beatitude
Statement 1: Beatific means to win against someone.
Statement 2: Beatitude means to be supremely blessed
solution: Beatific means showing or imparting supreme blessed happiness, as in a beatific smile, so statement 1 is wrong in confusing it with beat, meaning to defeat someone. Beatitude is correctly glossed as the state of being supremely blessed. Matches option C.

stem: Egress and Egressive
optA: Egress is a noun meaning a way out; Egressive is a noun meaning the act of leaving.
optB: Egress is a verb meaning to trap inside; Egressive is a noun meaning a blockage.
optC: Egress is a noun meaning an exit or means of departure; Egressive is an adjective meaning tending to go out or away.
optD: Egress is an adjective meaning outgoing; Egressive is a verb meaning to exile.
solution: Egress is a noun meaning an exit or a means of going out, while egressive is an adjective describing something that tends to go out or away. The other options misstate the part of speech of one word or of both. Matches option C.

stem: Complaisant and Complaisance
optA: Complaisant is a verb meaning to comply reluctantly; Complaisance is a noun meaning resistance.
optB: Complaisant is a noun meaning generosity; Complaisance is an adjective meaning flexible.
optC: Complaisant is an adjective meaning eager to please or obliging; Complaisance is a noun meaning a disposition to please or oblige.
optD: Complaisant is an adjective meaning harshly critical; Complaisance is a noun meaning aggression.
solution: Complaisant is an adjective meaning eager to please or obliging, and complaisance is the matching noun naming that disposition. Both the meaning and the part of speech must be right, and only one option gets both halves correct. Matches option C.

stem: Redound and Redundant
optA: Redound is a noun meaning repetition; Redundant is a verb meaning to echo.
optB: Redound is a verb meaning to contribute greatly (to credit or discredit); Redundant is an adjective meaning superfluous or excessively repetitive.
optC: Redound is an adjective meaning loud; Redundant is a noun meaning a copy.
optD: Redound is a noun meaning a mistake; Redundant is a verb meaning to summarize.
solution: Redound is a verb meaning to contribute greatly to someone's credit or discredit, as in the result redounds to his honour. Redundant is an adjective meaning superfluous or needlessly repetitive. Matches option B.

stem: Cavil and Caviling
optA: Cavil is a noun meaning a petty objection; Caviling is a verb meaning to raise trivial criticisms.
optB: Cavil is a verb meaning to praise; Caviling is a noun meaning generous feedback.
optC: Cavil is an adjective meaning insignificant; Caviling is a noun meaning determination.
optD: Cavil is a noun meaning intense support; Caviling is a verb meaning to applaud.
solution: Cavil as a noun is a petty or frivolous objection, and as a verb it means to raise such trivial criticisms, which is the sense the form caviling carries. Every other option reverses the meaning into praise or support. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Caviling is a participle form, so it also serves as an adjective, as in a caviling critic; labelling it simply a verb is loose but defensible, since it is the -ing form of the verb cavil. No other option has either half right, so A is the only viable key.

stem: Gait and Gate
optA: Gait is a noun meaning to open an entrance. Gate is a noun meaning a way of walking.
optB: Gait is a noun meaning a manner of walking. Gate is a noun meaning a hinged barrier.
optC: Gait is an adjective meaning slow. Gate is a noun meaning entrance.
optD: Gait is an adjective meaning pace. Gate is an adjective meaning unless.
solution: Gait is a noun meaning a manner or style of walking, while gate is a noun meaning a hinged barrier at an entrance. The first option swaps the two meanings. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 16e6a925-d977-4454-a9f7-344ced376f9e (same word set, same task); option text differs, so the key is derived here rather than copied.

stem:
Farther, Further
1. The soldiers marched farther into the desert.
2. We need to discuss this issue further before making a decision.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Farther is used for physical distance covered, while further is used for figurative or additional extent, such as more discussion. Both sentences observe the distinction. Matches option C.

stem:
Perquisite, Prerequisite
1. A company car is one of the perquisites of the job.
2. A degree in economics is a perquisite for this position.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: A perquisite is a benefit or perk attached to a job, while a prerequisite is something required in advance as a condition. Sentence 1 is right, but sentence 2 needs prerequisite, since a degree is a condition of eligibility and not a perk. Matches option A.

stem:
Pragmatic, Dogmatic
1. The leader adopted a pragmatic approach to solve the crisis.
2. He remained pragmatic and refused to consider any other viewpoint.
In which sentences are the words used correctly?
solution: Pragmatic means practical and focused on what actually works, so sentence 1 is correct. Sentence 2 describes someone rigidly clinging to a fixed position and refusing all other viewpoints, which is dogmatic rather than pragmatic, so only sentence 1 uses its word correctly. Matches option A.

stem: Allay and Alleviate
optA: Allay is a verb meaning to worsen; Alleviate is a verb meaning to intensify.
optB: Allay is a verb meaning to reduce fear or anxiety; Alleviate is a verb meaning to make suffering less severe.
optC: Allay is a noun meaning calm; Alleviate is an adjective meaning mild.
optD: Allay is a verb meaning delay; Alleviate is a noun meaning relief.
solution: Allay is a verb meaning to calm or reduce fear, doubt or anxiety, and alleviate is a verb meaning to make pain or suffering less severe. Option A inverts both senses to worsen and intensify, which is the opposite of what each word does. Matches option B.

stem: Refractory and Refraction
optA: Refractory is an adjective meaning stubborn or resistant; Refraction is a noun meaning bending of light.
optB: Refractory is a noun meaning resistance; Refraction is a verb meaning to break.
optC: Refractory is an adjective meaning flexible; Refraction is an adjective meaning distorted.
optD: Refractory is a verb meaning resist; Refraction is a noun meaning division.
solution: Refractory is an adjective meaning stubborn, unmanageable or resistant to treatment, while refraction is a noun for the bending of light or sound as it passes from one medium into another. Option D fails on both halves, turning refractory into a verb and glossing refraction as division rather than bending. Matches option A.

stem: Mitigate and Militate
optA: Mitigate is a noun meaning reduction; Militate is a noun meaning resistance.
optB: Mitigate is a verb meaning to make less severe; Militate is a verb meaning to have force or effect.
optC: Mitigate is a verb meaning to oppose strongly; Militate is a verb meaning to soften.
optD: Mitigate is an adjective meaning mild; Militate is an adjective meaning aggressive.
solution: Mitigate is a verb meaning to make something less severe or painful, and militate is a verb meaning to have weight or influence, normally in the phrase militate against. Option C swaps the two, giving mitigate the sense of opposing and militate the sense of softening. Matches option B.
reviewNote: The gloss have force or effect for militate is loose but not wrong. Militate is almost always intransitive with against or in favour of, so a fuller gloss would be to be a powerful factor in preventing or bringing something about. No other option is defensible, so the key is not in doubt.

stem: Specious and Speculative
optA: Specious is an adjective meaning doubtful; Speculative is an adjective meaning deceptive.
optB: Specious is an adjective meaning superficially plausible but actually misleading; Speculative is an adjective meaning based on conjecture rather than knowledge.
optC: Specious is a noun meaning argument; Speculative is a verb meaning to assume.
optD: Specious is an adjective meaning theoretical; Speculative is a noun meaning risk.
solution: Specious is an adjective describing an argument that looks convincing on the surface but is actually false, and speculative is an adjective meaning based on guesswork rather than firm evidence. Option A weakens specious to merely doubtful and then wrongly hands speculative the deceptive sense that belongs to specious. Matches option B.

stem: Disinterested and Uninterested
optA: Disinterested is a noun meaning neutrality; Uninterested is a verb meaning ignore.
optB: Disinterested is an adjective meaning impartial; Uninterested is an adjective meaning lacking interest.
optC: Disinterested is an adjective meaning lacking interest; Uninterested is an adjective meaning impartial.
optD: Disinterested is an adjective meaning bored; Uninterested is a noun meaning apathy.
solution: Disinterested is an adjective meaning impartial or free from personal stake, while uninterested is an adjective meaning simply not interested or bored. Option C is the classic trap, reversing the pair so that disinterested is glossed as lacking interest. Matches option B.

stem: Momentous and Momentary
optA: Momentous is an adjective meaning brief; Momentary is an adjective meaning significant.
optB: Momentous is an adjective meaning significant; Momentary is an adjective meaning lasting for a short time.
optC: Momentous is a noun meaning importance; Momentary is a verb meaning to pause.
optD: Momentous is an adjective meaning delayed; Momentary is a noun meaning instant.
solution: Momentous is an adjective meaning of great importance or consequence, and momentary is an adjective meaning lasting only a moment. Option A reverses them, calling momentous brief and momentary significant. Matches option B.

stem: Impugn and Impute
optA: Impugn is a verb meaning to attribute; Impute is a verb meaning to challenge.
optB: Impugn is a verb meaning to question the truth or integrity; Impute is a verb meaning to attribute (often blame).
optC: Impugn is a noun meaning doubt; Impute is a noun meaning blame.
optD: Impugn is a verb meaning to prove; Impute is an adjective meaning assumed.
solution: Impugn is a verb meaning to attack or call into question a person's truthfulness or integrity, and impute is a verb meaning to attribute something, usually a fault or blame, to someone. Option A swaps the two, giving impugn the attributing sense that belongs to impute. Matches option B.

stem: Pedantic and Didactic
optA: Pedantic is an adjective meaning instructive; Didactic is an adjective meaning trivial.
optB: Pedantic is an adjective meaning overly concerned with minor details; Didactic is an adjective meaning intended to teach.
optC: Pedantic is a noun meaning teacher; Didactic is a verb meaning instruct.
optD: Pedantic is an adjective meaning moral; Didactic is a noun meaning lesson.
solution: Pedantic is an adjective describing someone fussily preoccupied with minor rules and details, while didactic is an adjective meaning designed to teach or instruct. Option A exchanges the two glosses, labelling pedantic as instructive and didactic as trivial. Matches option B.

stem: Recondite and Condign
optA: Recondite is an adjective meaning difficult to understand; Condign is an adjective meaning appropriate or deserved (especially punishment).
optB: Recondite is a noun meaning secrecy; Condign is a verb meaning to punish.
optC: Recondite is an adjective meaning concealed physically; Condign is an adjective meaning excessive.
optD: Recondite is a verb meaning obscure; Condign is a noun meaning justice.
solution: Recondite is an adjective meaning abstruse and hard for an ordinary reader to understand, and condign is an adjective meaning fitting and deserved, used almost always of punishment. Option C misreads recondite as physically hidden and turns condign, which means proportionate, into its opposite, excessive. Matches option A.

stem: Truculent and Truncate
optA: Truculent is a verb meaning threaten; Truncate is an adjective meaning brief.
optB: Truculent is a noun meaning anger; Truncate is a noun meaning fragment.
optC: Truculent is an adjective meaning calm; Truncate is a verb meaning extend.
optD: Truculent is an adjective meaning aggressively defiant; Truncate is a verb meaning to shorten by cutting.
solution: Truculent is an adjective meaning aggressively defiant or belligerent, and truncate is a verb meaning to shorten something by cutting off a part of it. Option C reverses both, calling truculent calm and truncate extend. Matches option D.

stem: Pellucid and Pelagic
optA: Pellucid is a noun meaning clarity; Pelagic is a verb meaning float.
optB: Pellucid is an adjective meaning clear or easily understood; Pelagic is an adjective relating to the open sea.
optC: Pellucid is an adjective meaning dim; Pelagic is an adjective meaning coastal.
optD: Pellucid is a verb meaning clarify; Pelagic is a noun meaning ocean.
solution: Pellucid is an adjective meaning transparently clear, whether of water or of prose, and pelagic is an adjective relating to the open sea away from the coast. Option C is wrong twice over, making pellucid dim and confining pelagic to the coast, which is the very region the word excludes. Matches option B.

stem: Malinger and Meander
optA: Malinger is a verb meaning to fake illness; Meander is a verb meaning to wander aimlessly.
optB: Malinger is a noun meaning illness; Meander is an adjective meaning indirect.
optC: Malinger is a verb meaning delay; Meander is a noun meaning confusion.
optD: Malinger is an adjective meaning weak; Meander is a verb meaning decide.
solution: Malinger is a verb meaning to pretend to be ill in order to escape work or duty, and meander is a verb meaning to follow a winding course or wander without direction. Option C loses the deliberate deception in malinger by reducing it to delay, and demotes meander to a noun. Matches option A.

stem: Noetic and Numinous
optA: Noetic is a noun meaning knowledge; Numinous is a verb meaning inspire.
optB: Noetic is an adjective relating to intellect; Numinous is an adjective meaning spiritually mysterious.
optC: Noetic is an adjective meaning emotional; Numinous is an adjective meaning logical.
optD: Noetic is a verb meaning think; Numinous is a noun meaning divinity.
solution: Noetic is an adjective relating to the mind or the intellect, and numinous is an adjective meaning filled with a sense of the divine or spiritually mysterious. Option C swaps their fields entirely, making noetic emotional and numinous logical. Matches option B.

stem: Palliative and Palliate
optA: Palliative is an adjective meaning soothing without curing; Palliate is a verb meaning to lessen severity.
optB: Palliative is a noun meaning cure; Palliate is a verb meaning intensify.
optC: Palliative is a verb meaning comfort; Palliate is a noun meaning relief.
optD: Palliative is an adjective meaning permanent; Palliate is an adjective meaning mild.
solution: Palliative is an adjective describing treatment that eases symptoms without curing the underlying disease, and palliate is the verb meaning to lessen the severity of pain or of an offence. Option B breaks both halves, since palliative care is defined by not curing, and palliate means to reduce rather than to intensify. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Palliative is also a well established noun meaning a remedy that relieves without curing, so the adjective label describes only its primary use. That use is the standard one and no other option is defensible, so the key stands.

stem: Explicate and Implicate
optA: Explicate is an adjective meaning clear; Implicate is a noun meaning guilt.
optB: Explicate is a verb meaning to explain; Implicate is a verb meaning to involve or show connection.
optC: Explicate is a noun meaning explanation; Implicate is an adjective meaning implied.
optD: Explicate is a verb meaning to confuse; Implicate is a verb meaning to explain.
solution: Explicate is a verb meaning to analyse and explain something in detail, and implicate is a verb meaning to show that someone or something is involved, often in a crime. Option D inverts explicate to confuse and then gives implicate the explaining sense that belongs to explicate. Matches option B.

stem: Torpid and Turgid
optA: Torpid is an adjective meaning sluggish; Turgid is an adjective meaning swollen or overly ornate.
optB: Torpid is a noun meaning laziness; Turgid is a verb meaning swell.
optC: Torpid is an adjective meaning active; Turgid is an adjective meaning simple.
optD: Torpid is a verb meaning sleep; Turgid is a noun meaning excess.
solution: Torpid is an adjective meaning mentally or physically sluggish and inactive, and turgid is an adjective meaning swollen, or by extension pompous and overblown in style. Option C reverses both, describing torpid as active and turgid as simple. Matches option A.

stem: Repudiate and Reprobate
optA: Repudiate is a verb meaning reject; Reprobate is a noun meaning morally unprincipled person.
optB: Repudiate is a noun meaning denial; Reprobate is a verb meaning approve.
optC: Repudiate is an adjective meaning false; Reprobate is an adjective meaning moral.
optD: Repudiate is a verb meaning accept; Reprobate is a noun meaning praise.
solution: Repudiate is a verb meaning to reject or refuse to accept something such as a claim, a debt or an agreement, and reprobate is a noun for an unprincipled or morally dissolute person. Option D reverses repudiate to accept and turns reprobate, a term of censure, into praise. Matches option A.

stem: Extemporaneous and Contemporaneous
optA: Extemporaneous is an adjective meaning occurring at the same time; Contemporaneous is an adjective meaning spontaneous.
optB: Extemporaneous is an adjective meaning improvised; Contemporaneous is an adjective meaning existing at the same time.
optC: Extemporaneous is a noun meaning speech; Contemporaneous is a verb meaning coexist.
optD: Extemporaneous is an adjective meaning planned; Contemporaneous is an adjective meaning delayed
solution: Extemporaneous is an adjective meaning spoken or done on the spur of the moment without preparation, and contemporaneous is an adjective meaning existing or occurring at the same time. One distractor swaps the pair, and another goes further by calling extemporaneous planned, which is its opposite. Matches option B.

stem: Incipient and Insipid
optA: Incipient is a noun meaning start; Insipid is a verb meaning bore.
optB: Incipient is an adjective meaning beginning; Insipid is an adjective meaning lacking flavor or interest.
optC: Incipient is an adjective meaning dull; Insipid is an adjective meaning energetic.
optD: Incipient is a verb meaning begin; Insipid is a noun meaning taste.
solution: Incipient is an adjective meaning just beginning to appear or develop, and insipid is an adjective meaning tasteless, or dull and lacking interest. Option C reverses them, giving incipient the dull sense of insipid and then calling insipid energetic. Matches option B.

stem:
S1: What is \(\underline{\text{especially}}\) noticeable about the pair is that they always dress impeccably.
S2: Lunch is served late in the office, \(\underline{\text{specially}}\) on days when there is a board meeting.
optA: S1 is right and S2 is wrong
optB: S1 is wrong and S2 is right
optC: Both S1 and S2 are wrong
optD: Both S1 and S2 are right
solution: Especially means particularly or above all, while specially means for one specific purpose. S1 uses especially correctly for what is particularly noticeable, but S2 is describing degree, not purpose, so it needs especially on days when there is a board meeting. Matches option A.

stem:
S1: The matter was resolved amicably \(\underline{\text{between}}\) the group even though there were so many of them.
S2: \(\underline{\text{Among}}\) them the two never have problems sharing what they have.
optA: S1 is right and S2 is wrong
optB: S1 is wrong and S2 is right
optC: Both S1 and S2 are wrong
optD: Both S1 and S2 are right
solution: Between is used of two or of a small number of separately identified people, and among is used of an undifferentiated group. S1 says between the group when there were so many of them, where among belongs, and S2 says among them the two, where between belongs, so the two sentences carry mirror-image errors. Matches option C.

stem:
S1: We \(\underline{\text{shall}}\) have to present ourselves before the Dean and explain our behaviour.
S2: They \(\underline{\text{will}}\) need to get their act together if they wish to win the contract.
optA: S1 is right and S2 is wrong
optB: S1 is wrong and S2 is right
optC: Both S1 and S2 are wrong
optD: Both S1 and S2 are right
solution: In traditional usage plain future takes shall with the first person and will with the second and third. S1 has we shall and S2 has they will, so both follow the rule. Matches option D. The alternative that rejects they will is wrong, because that is the standard third-person future.

stem:
S1: I have not seen her \(\underline{\text{since}}\) a long time.
S2: It has been a while \(\underline{\text{since}}\) I saw her.
optA: S1 is right and S2 is wrong
optB: S1 is wrong and S2 is right
optC: Both S1 and S2 are wrong
optD: Both S1 and S2 are right
solution: Since fixes the point at which something started, whereas for measures a stretch of time. S1 says since a long time, which names a duration and should read for a long time, while S2 uses since correctly before the past-simple clause I saw her. Matches option B. Treating both sentences as right would require accepting the duration reading of since.
reviewNote: S2 was judged independently rather than assumed right: it has been a while since plus a past simple clause is standard idiom, so only S1 fails and C (both wrong) was rejected.

stem:
S1: The teacher enquired whether there is \(\underline{\text{any}}\) problem with the question paper.
S2: He asked her whether she had \(\underline{\text{some}}\) pets at home.
optA: S1 is right and S2 is wrong
optB: S1 is wrong and S2 is right
optC: Both S1 and S2 are wrong
optD: Both S1 and S2 are right
solution: Any is the normal choice in questions, negatives and after whether, while some belongs in plain affirmative statements. S1's whether there is any problem is correct, but S2's whether she had some pets should read any pets. Matches option A. Treating both sentences as right would accept some inside an indirect question.
reviewNote: Some in a question is idiomatic when the speaker is offering something or expects the answer yes, so S2 is defensible in conversational English; rejected because the item is testing the prescriptive any-in-questions rule and only that reading gives a single correct option.
